title: Genesis 21. The Cup of Laughter.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 21. The Cup of Laughter.
The Lord visited Sarah as He had said.
And the Lord did to Sarah as He had spoken.
The Cup that was promised in chapter seventeen,
that was laughed at in chapter eighteen,
that was endangered in chapter twenty, arrives.
What was spoken by voice is now flesh.
What was counted in stars is now held in arms.
Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age,
at the set time of which God had spoken.
Abraham called the name of his son who was born to him,
whom Sarah bore to him, Isaac.
Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when he was eight days old,
as God had commanded him.
Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.
At the set time.
Not early.
Not late.
At the set time,
the same word used when God told Abraham in chapter seventeen:
at this set time in the next year.
The Cup does not arrive when the vessel wants it.
It arrives when the One who fills it decides.
The man who was seventy-five when he left Haran is a hundred when the son is born.
Twenty-five years of sojourning.
Twenty-five years of altars and famine and Egypt and arrangement and covenant and circumcision and laughter and silence.
And then, at the set time, a son.
Sarah says: God has made laughter for me.
Everyone who hears will laugh with me.
The laughter that was doubt in chapter seventeen,
Abraham falling on his face, laughing, saying:
Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?
and the laughter that was denial in chapter eighteen,
Sarah laughing behind the tent flap, then lying about it,
has become the laughter of fulfillment.
The same word.
The same root.
laughter.
The sound that was disbelief is now the sound of a woman holding what she was told she could not hold.
The Cup that was met with laughter is now filled by it.
Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children?
For I have borne him a son in his old age.
The child grows.
He is weaned.
Abraham makes a great feast on the day Isaac is weaned.
The Cup of promise is celebrated.
The son of laughter has survived infancy.
The household that was divided between the son of arrangement and the son of promise gathers for a feast.
The Cup that was cut in blood and sealed in flesh now sits at a table.
But Sarah sees.
The son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she bore to Abraham, laughing.
Mocking.
The same word.
laughter.
But this laughter is not joy.
The son of arrangement laughs at the son of promise.
Ishmael, the wild donkey, the one whose hand is against everyone,
turns his laughter toward the child who carries the covenant.
The word that named Isaac now names what Ishmael does to him.
Sarah says: Cast out this slave woman and her son.
For the son of this slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.
The Cup that was filled by arrangement is now cast out by the woman who arranged it.
Sarah, who gave Hagar to Abraham in chapter sixteen,
now demands that Hagar be thrown out in chapter twenty-one.
The arrangement that was meant to produce the promise is now treated as a threat to it.
The woman who said Perhaps I shall obtain children by her now says:
He shall not be heir with my son.
The thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight on account of his son.
He has held Ishmael for thirteen years.
He circumcised him with his own hands.
He asked God to let Ishmael live before Him.
The father who loves both sons is being asked to send one away.
God speaks:
Do not be displeased because of the boy and because of your slave woman.
Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice.
For through Isaac shall your offspring be named.
And I will also make a nation of the son of the slave woman,
because he is your offspring.
God sides with Sarah.
Not because Sarah is right in her motives,
the woman who arranged the arrangement now demands its removal.
But because the covenant must be carried by Isaac, not Ishmael.
The Cup of arrangement must be separated from the Cup of promise.
Not destroyed.
Not abandoned.
Separated.
Ishmael will be a nation.
He will not be heir.
The distinction is not cruelty.
It is purpose.
The Cup that carries the word God spoke when He walked alone through the pieces cannot be shared with the cup that was filled by human will.
Abraham rises early in the morning.
He takes bread and a skin of water and puts it on Hagar's shoulder.
He gives her the child.
And sends her away.
She departs.
She wanders in the wilderness of Beersheba.
The water in the skin is spent.
She puts the child under one of the shrubs.
She goes and sits down opposite him, a bow shot away.
She says: Let me not see the death of the child.
She sits opposite him and lifts up her voice and weeps.
The same wilderness.
The same spring.
The same woman.
In chapter sixteen, Hagar fled from Sarai,
and the Angel of the Lord found her by a spring on the way to Shur.
She named God El Roi, the God who sees me.
Now she is in the wilderness again, not fleeing but sent.
Not alone but with a child.
Not pregnant but watching him die.
The Cup of arrangement that God blessed has run out of water.
God heard the voice of the boy.
Not Hagar's voice.
The boy's.
The same verb used in chapter sixteen, God heard,
the name Ishmael means God hears.
But in chapter sixteen, God heard Hagar's affliction.
Here, God hears the boy's voice.
The son who was named God-hears is heard by God.
The arrangement that produced him has been cast out.
The water is gone.
The mother is weeping.
But the boy is heard.
The Angel of God calls to Hagar from heaven: What troubles you,
Hagar?
Do not be afraid.
God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.
Get up.
Lift up the boy.
Hold him with your hand,
for I will make him a great nation.
God opens her eyes.
She sees a well of water.
She goes, fills the skin, and gives the boy a drink.
The Cup that was drained in the wilderness is refilled.
The well was there, she had not seen it.
The same God who opened the fountains of the deep in chapter seven and closed them in chapter eight now opens the eyes of a woman in a wilderness.
What she needed was already in the ground.
She had not seen it.
God opened her eyes.
God was with the boy.
He grew.
He lived in the wilderness and became an archer.
He lived in the wilderness of Paran.
His mother got him a wife from the land of Egypt.
God was with the boy.
The son of arrangement, the one who was not the promise,
is not abandoned.
God is with him.
The same presence that was with Abraham is with Ishmael.
The boy who was cast out grows.
The wild donkey finds his range.
The archer lives in the wilderness.
His mother, the Egyptian, brings him an Egyptian wife.
The arrangement that began with an Egyptian servant ends with an Egyptian marriage.
The Cup of arrangement does not disappear.
It becomes a nation.
A different nation.
A nation that will stand over against the nation of the promise.
But not forgotten.
Not unprovided for.
God was with the boy.
Then Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, speak to Abraham:
God is with you in all that you do.
Now swear to me by God that you will not deal falsely with me or my son or my grandson.
As I have shown kindness to you,
show kindness to me and to the land in which you have sojourned.
The king who was deceived by Abraham in chapter twenty now recognizes that God is with him.
The man who lied about his wife is now asked to swear an oath of honesty.
The pagan king has learned what the prophet's integrity looks like,
or what it does not look like,
and still wants a covenant with him.
Not because Abraham is trustworthy.
Because God is with him.
Abraham swears.
But he also confronts Abimelech about a well that Abimelech's servants had seized by force.
Abimelech says: I do not know who did this.
You did not tell me.
I heard of it only today.
Abraham takes sheep and cattle and gives them to Abimelech.
They make a covenant.
Abraham sets seven ewe lambs aside by themselves.
Abimelech asks: What do these seven ewe lambs mean?
Abraham says: You shall take them from my hand,
that they may be a witness that I dug this well.
Therefore the place is called Beersheba, Well of the Oath,
or Well of Seven.
The Cup of covenant between men is sealed at a well.
The same element that sustained Hagar in the wilderness now sustains a treaty between a prophet and a king.
Water is the witness.
Abraham plants a tamarisk tree in Beersheba.
And there he called on the name of the Lord,
the Everlasting God.
El Olam.
The Everlasting God.
The first time this name appears in Scripture.
The man who has walked with God for twenty-five years now knows Him as the One who does not end.
The Cup that was given in time, at the set time,
is held by the One who is outside time.
The promise that arrived when it was ready was spoken by the One who was ready before the promise was needed.
Abraham sojourns in the land of the Philistines for many days.
The Cup of laughter holds.
The promise has arrived.
The son of the arrangement has been cast out, not destroyed,
not forgotten, but sent away with a promise of his own.
The well in the wilderness and the well at Beersheba both bear witness:
God provides water where His word has placed people.
The Cup that was cut in blood, sealed in flesh,
endangered by fear, filled by arrangement, and finally received by faith, holds.
At the set time.
In the hands of a hundred-year-old man and a ninety-year-old woman and a child named Laughter.
What was spoken has become what is held.
The promise is no longer a word.
It is a boy.
